title: Rate limiter
scopeHtml: Scope: Token bucket, sliding window log and counter, pluggable strategies, per-key concurrency. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a rate limiter that decides, for each request key (user id, IP, API key), whether to allow or reject it, with the algorithm pluggable: token bucket, sliding window log, sliding window counter.

Clarify: limit per what (user, IP, endpoint)? What numbers (for example 100 requests per minute)? Is burst allowed? Single machine or distributed? Reject with HTTP 429 plus Retry-After? Fail open or closed if the limiter breaks? (Here: in-process, per-key, one interface, three strategies.)

Worked example. Limit 5 requests/s with burst 5: a client sends 10 at once; 5 pass, 5 get 429; two seconds later 2 more tokens exist if refill is 1/s. At a gateway taking 50,000 requests/s, a single abusive client sending 5,000/s would eat 10% of capacity without a limiter.

Industry examples. Stripe (token bucket on requests, plus concurrency limiters), GitHub API (5,000 requests/hour per token with X-RateLimit-* headers), Cloudflare, NGINX limit_req (leaky bucket), AWS API Gateway (token bucket), Envoy and Kong global rate-limit services backed by Redis.

Everyday analogy. A bouncer who lets in at most N people per minute, and the queue outside keeps its own count per group.

Common interview traps.

  • Not asking per-what. A global limit is a different design from per-user.
  • Forgetting the response contract: 429 and Retry-After.
  • Skipping the fail-open vs fail-closed discussion.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• RateLimiter (interface): allow(): boolean. One instance guards one key.
  • TokenBucket, SlidingWindowLog, SlidingWindowCounter: strategies.
  • RateLimiterService: map from key to limiter, created on first use through a factory.
  • Clock (LongSupplier): injected for testability.

Design choice: each limiter object holds the state for one key, and the service owns the key map. That keeps the algorithms tiny (no key handling) and makes the lock per key.

Decision gravity. The allow() interface is the one-way door; algorithms behind it can be changed per route or per customer tier without touching callers. Per-key state in memory is reversible to a Redis-backed version by swapping the factory.

Everyday analogy. Every customer has their own punch card; the shop only needs to look at that card, not at everyone's.

Common interview traps.

  • A single global counter shared by all users.
  • Algorithms that need a timer thread per key (millions of keys). Prefer lazy computation on each call.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
<<interface>>
   +--------------------+
   | RateLimiter        |
   | allow(): boolean   |
   +--------------------+
     ^        ^         ^
+-----------+ +------------------+ +----------------------+
|TokenBucket| |SlidingWindowLog  | |SlidingWindowCounter  |
| capacity  | | limit,windowMs   | | limit,windowMs       |
| refill/ms | | stamps: Deque    | | cur, prev, curStart  |
| tokens    | +------------------+ +----------------------+
| last      |
+-----------+

+--------------------------------------+
| RateLimiterService                   |
| byKey: ConcurrentHashMap<key,Limiter>|
| factory: Supplier<RateLimiter>       |
| allow(key): boolean                  |
+--------------------------------------+

How to read it. The service holds the factory, so the same service class can be used with any strategy by passing () -> new TokenBucket(...).

Common interview traps.

  • Passing the clock as a static System.currentTimeMillis(); tests then need sleep.
  • Mixing the key map into each algorithm.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Strategy (RateLimiter): algorithms are interchangeable. Why: different endpoints want different behaviour (login: strict; search: burst friendly). Alternative: one class with a mode enum (grows branches). Reversible.
  • Factory (Supplier<RateLimiter>): the service creates a limiter per key, without knowing the concrete type.
  • Lazy refill: compute the new token count from elapsed time on each call; no background timer. O(1) per call, O(1) memory per key.

Comparison (the table interviewers love):

Algorithm Memory per key Accuracy Allows bursts Notes
Fixed window counter 1 counter Poor at window edges (2x burst across a boundary) Yes, at edges Simplest; Redis INCR + EXPIRE
Sliding window log one timestamp per request (up to the limit) Exact No Memory heavy for large limits
Sliding window counter 2 counters Approximate (assumes even spread in the previous window) Mild Cloudflare reported this to be very accurate in practice
Token bucket 2 numbers (tokens, last time) Exact for its model Yes, up to capacity Common default (Stripe, AWS)
Leaky bucket a queue or counter Smooths output rate No NGINX limit_req

Worked example (sliding window counter). Limit 10 per 1,000 ms. Previous window had 10 requests, current window is 50% elapsed, current count 0. Estimate = 10 x 0.5 + 0 = 5, so 5 more are allowed, matching the test.

Everyday analogy. Token bucket: a jar that gains a coin every second (max 5) and each visit spends one. Sliding log: a notebook listing exact visit times from the last minute.

Common interview traps.

  • Fixed window edge case: 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:00 are both "allowed" but that is 200 in two seconds.
  • Claiming sliding window counter is exact. It is an estimate.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable file Main.java (three strategies, per-key service, tests including a concurrent one):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.function.*;

/** Strategy interface: one instance guards ONE key (user, IP, API key). */
interface RateLimiter {
    boolean allow();
}

/** Token bucket: allows bursts up to capacity, long-run rate = refillPerSec. Lazy refill, no timer thread. */
class TokenBucket implements RateLimiter {
    private final double capacity, refillPerMs; private final LongSupplier clock;
    private double tokens; private long last;
    TokenBucket(int capacity, double refillPerSec, LongSupplier clock) {
        this.capacity = capacity; this.refillPerMs = refillPerSec / 1000.0; this.clock = clock;
        this.tokens = capacity; this.last = clock.getAsLong();
    }
    public synchronized boolean allow() {
        long now = clock.getAsLong();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - last) * refillPerMs);
        last = now;
        if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return true; }
        return false;
    }
}

/** Sliding window log: exact, but stores one timestamp per accepted request (memory = limit). */
class SlidingWindowLog implements RateLimiter {
    private final int limit; private final long windowMs; private final LongSupplier clock;
    private final ArrayDeque<Long> stamps = new ArrayDeque<>();
    SlidingWindowLog(int limit, long windowMs, LongSupplier clock) { this.limit = limit; this.windowMs = windowMs; this.clock = clock; }
    public synchronized boolean allow() {
        long now = clock.getAsLong();
        while (!stamps.isEmpty() && stamps.peekFirst() <= now - windowMs) stamps.pollFirst();
        if (stamps.size() >= limit) return false;
        stamps.addLast(now);
        return true;
    }
}

/** Sliding window counter: two counters, weighted estimate. O(1) memory, small approximation error. */
class SlidingWindowCounter implements RateLimiter {
    private final int limit; private final long windowMs; private final LongSupplier clock;
    private long curStart; private int cur, prev;
    SlidingWindowCounter(int limit, long windowMs, LongSupplier clock) {
        this.limit = limit; this.windowMs = windowMs; this.clock = clock; this.curStart = clock.getAsLong();
    }
    public synchronized boolean allow() {
        long now = clock.getAsLong();
        long elapsedWindows = (now - curStart) / windowMs;
        if (elapsedWindows >= 1) {                       // roll the window forward
            prev = elapsedWindows == 1 ? cur : 0;
            cur = 0; curStart += elapsedWindows * windowMs;
        }
        double fractionOfPrev = 1.0 - (double) (now - curStart) / windowMs;
        if (prev * fractionOfPrev + cur >= limit) return false;
        cur++;
        return true;
    }
}

/** Per-key registry. computeIfAbsent is atomic so two threads never create two buckets for one key. */
class RateLimiterService {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateLimiter> byKey = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Supplier<RateLimiter> factory;
    RateLimiterService(Supplier<RateLimiter> factory) { this.factory = factory; }
    boolean allow(String key) { return byKey.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> factory.get()).allow(); }
}

public class Main {
    static void check(boolean c, String msg) { if (!c) throw new AssertionError(msg); }
    static int run(RateLimiter rl, int n) { int ok = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (rl.allow()) ok++; return ok; }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        long[] t = {0}; LongSupplier clock = () -> t[0];

        RateLimiter tb = new TokenBucket(5, 1.0, clock);              // burst 5, then 1/sec
        check(run(tb, 10) == 5, "burst of 5");
        t[0] += 2000;
        check(run(tb, 10) == 2, "2 tokens refilled after 2s");

        t[0] = 0; RateLimiter log = new SlidingWindowLog(3, 1000, clock);
        check(run(log, 5) == 3, "3 per window");
        t[0] = 999; check(!log.allow(), "still inside window");
        t[0] = 1000; check(log.allow(), "oldest aged out");

        t[0] = 0; RateLimiter swc = new SlidingWindowCounter(10, 1000, clock);
        check(run(swc, 10) == 10, "fills window");
        t[0] = 1500;                                                  // half of previous window still counts: 10*0.5=5
        check(run(swc, 10) == 5, "weighted estimate allows 5 more");

        // pluggable + concurrent: 1 key, 200 threads-worth of calls, capacity 50, no refill => exactly 50 pass
        RateLimiterService svc = new RateLimiterService(() -> new TokenBucket(50, 0, () -> 0L));
        AtomicInteger allowed = new AtomicInteger();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) pool.submit(() -> { if (svc.allow("user-1")) allowed.incrementAndGet(); });
        pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        check(allowed.get() == 50, "exactly 50, got " + allowed.get());
        check(svc.allow("user-2"), "other keys are independent");
        System.out.println("P11 OK");
    }
}

The core in Kotlin:

fun interface RateLimiter { fun allow(): Boolean }

class TokenBucket(private val capacity: Int, refillPerSec: Double,
                  private val clock: () -> Long) : RateLimiter {
    private val refillPerMs = refillPerSec / 1000.0
    private var tokens = capacity.toDouble()
    private var last = clock()

    @Synchronized override fun allow(): Boolean {
        val now = clock()
        tokens = minOf(capacity.toDouble(), tokens + (now - last) * refillPerMs)
        last = now
        return if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; true } else false
    }
}

class SlidingWindowLog(private val limit: Int, private val windowMs: Long,
                       private val clock: () -> Long) : RateLimiter {
    private val stamps = ArrayDeque<Long>()
    @Synchronized override fun allow(): Boolean {
        val now = clock()
        while (stamps.isNotEmpty() && stamps.first() <= now - windowMs) stamps.removeFirst()
        if (stamps.size >= limit) return false
        stamps.addLast(now); return true
    }
}

class RateLimiterService(private val factory: () -> RateLimiter) {
    private val byKey = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateLimiter>()
    fun allow(key: String) = byKey.computeIfAbsent(key) { factory() }.allow()
}

Walk-through (token bucket). Capacity 5, refill 1/s, clock 0: 5 calls pass (tokens 0). Call 6 fails. Clock jumps to 2,000 ms: tokens = min(5, 0 + 2000 x 0.001) = 2, so exactly 2 more pass.

Common interview traps.

  • Not capping tokens at capacity after a long idle (an hour of idle gives 3,600 tokens).
  • int math on time deltas overflowing; use long.
  • Using <= vs < at window boundaries inconsistently.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac Main.java && java -ea Main
# prints: P11 OK

The test drives a fake clock. Token bucket: burst of 5 passes, 2 more after 2 s. Sliding log: 3 per window, rejected at 999 ms, allowed at 1,000 ms when the oldest ages out. Sliding counter: weighted estimate lets exactly 5 through. Concurrency: 200 tasks on 8 threads hit one key whose bucket has capacity 50 and no refill; exactly 50 pass. A second key is unaffected.

Common interview traps.

  • Tests that rely on Thread.sleep; they are slow and flaky.
  • No test for two keys being independent.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Two layers of shared state:

  1. Inside one limiter: the read-modify-write of tokens is not atomic. Two threads could both read tokens = 1, both decrement, and both be allowed. Fix: synchronized on the limiter (per key, so different keys do not contend), or a CAS loop on an AtomicLong that packs tokens and timestamp. The test proves exactly 50 of 200 pass.
  2. The key map: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent is atomic per key, so two threads never create two limiters for one key (which would double the allowance). Keep the factory cheap; it runs inside the map's bin lock.

Going distributed. In-process limits multiply by the number of servers (10 servers each allowing 100/min gives 1,000/min). Options:

  • Central Redis with a Lua script (atomic): GET tokens, last; compute; SET with EXPIRE. One round trip of about 0.5 ms; at 100k keys/s one Redis handles it, shard by key hash beyond that. Stripe and many API gateways do this.
  • Local token slice + periodic sync: each node takes tokens from the central store in chunks of 10; cheaper, slightly over-admits.
  • Sticky routing: send a key's traffic to the same node (consistent hashing) and keep local state; fast but fails over poorly.

Fail open or closed? If Redis is down, rejecting all traffic is an outage caused by the limiter. Most public APIs fail open (allow) with an alert; login or payment endpoints may fail closed.

Memory: idle keys leak. Evict limiters not touched for a window (Caffeine cache with expireAfterAccess) or use Redis TTLs: 10M keys x about 100 bytes = about 1 GB.

Incident pattern. Clock skew between nodes with a timestamp-based limiter in Redis causes early or late resets; use the Redis server time (TIME in Lua), not client time.

Decision gravity. Choosing fail-open vs fail-closed is a business decision per endpoint; make it configurable from day one (easy to change later, painful to discover during an outage).

Everyday analogy. Several ticket counters sharing one sign saying how many tickets are left; if each had its own sign, you could sell the same last ticket at every counter.

Common interview traps.

  • Check-then-set in Redis with separate GET and SET (race); use Lua or INCR.
  • Using wall clock in tests and in production without a monotonic source for elapsed time (JVM: System.nanoTime is monotonic; wall-clock can jump).

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Tiered limits: free vs paid plans, via a limiter factory chosen by plan.
  • Multiple rules per request: per second AND per day; allow only if all pass (compose limiters).
  • Response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After; then allow() should return a result object with remaining and reset time.
  • Weighted requests: expensive endpoints cost more tokens (tryAcquire(n)).
  • Concurrency limiter: cap in-flight requests rather than rate (a semaphore).
  • Dynamic config: hot-reload limits without a deploy.
  • Load shedding vs rate limiting: shedding protects the server by priority under overload; limiting enforces fairness per client.

Common interview traps.

  • Returning only a boolean when the API needs Retry-After.
  • Limiting by IP only (NAT puts thousands of users behind one IP); combine with user or API key.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• One RateLimiter interface per key; strategies: token bucket (bursty, default), sliding log (exact, memory heavy), sliding counter (2 numbers, approximate), fixed window (edge-burst flaw).
  • Refill lazily from elapsed time; inject the clock; cap tokens at capacity.
  • Per-key synchronized plus ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent makes it thread-safe; the test proves exactly N of M requests pass.
  • Distributed: Redis plus Lua for atomicity, TTLs for cleanup, decide fail-open or fail-closed.
  • Always mention 429 and Retry-After, and what the key is.
